concepts: Locus in the Argand plane (modulus of a Möbius map of a real parameter)
questions.question: All the points in the set $S=\left\{\frac{\alpha+i}{\alpha-i}:\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\right\}$ $(i=\sqrt{-1})$ lie on a :
questions.key_idea: For real $\alpha$, $\alpha+i$ and $\alpha-i$ are conjugates, so the quotient has modulus 1.
solution: So every point lies on the circle $x^2+y^2=1$, whose radius is 1. Option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: For real $\alpha$ the numerator and denominator are complex conjugates, so $|w|=1$ at once.
solution: Hence $|w|=1$ for every real $\alpha$: all points lie on the unit circle (centre $0$, radius 1).
Cross-check: put $\alpha=\cot\theta$; then $w=\frac{\cos\theta+i\sin\theta}{\cos\theta-i\sin\theta}=e^{2i\theta}$, a point of the unit circle.

useful_results: $\left|\frac{z}{\bar z}\right|=1$ for every $z\ne0$; so $\frac{\alpha+i}{\alpha-i}$ ($\alpha$ real) always has modulus 1.
The map $\alpha\mapsto\frac{\alpha+i}{\alpha-i}$ (Cayley map) sends the real line onto the unit circle minus the point $1$ (it is the limit $\alpha\to\infty$).
Parametrisation: $\alpha=\cot\theta$ gives $e^{2i\theta}$; equivalently $\frac{1+it}{1-it}=e^{2i\tan^{-1}t}$.

concepts: Series: exponential series and sums of $\frac{1}{r!}$ over odd/even indices
questions.question: The sum of the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{n^2+6n+10}{(2n+1)!}$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Put $r=2n+1$ and write $r^2+10r+29=r(r-1)+11r+29$ so each part telescopes into a factorial series.
solution: Expand the numerator: $(r-1)^2+12(r-1)+40=r^2+10r+29$, so the sum is $\sum\frac{r^2+10r+29}{4\,r!}$.
questions.correction_note: PDF's second line reads $\frac{(r-1)^2+12(r-1)+10}{4\,r!}$; the constant must be 40 (since $4\cdot10=40$), not 10. The next line $r^2+10r+29$ is only correct with 40 ($1-12+40=29$), so the later working and the answer are unaffected. Series value checked numerically: 3.0574807.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $\sinh x=\sum_{m\ \mathrm{odd}}\frac{x^m}{m!}$ and apply $x^2\frac{d^2}{dx^2}$ and $x\frac{d}{dx}$ to produce $m(m-1)$ and $m$ in the numerator.
solution: With $m=2n+1$ (odd, $m\ge3$) the term is $\frac{m^2+10m+29}{4\,m!}$, as before.
This sum includes $m=1$, whose term is $\frac{1+10+29}{1!}=40$; remove it: $\sum_{m\ge3}=30\sinh1+11\cosh1-40$.

useful_results: $\sum_{r\ \mathrm{odd}}\frac{1}{r!}=\sinh1=\frac{e-e^{-1}}{2}$ and $\sum_{r\ \mathrm{even}\ge0}\frac1{r!}=\cosh1=\frac{e+e^{-1}}{2}$; remember to subtract the first terms when the sum starts later.
For $\sum\frac{P(r)}{r!}$ write $P(r)$ in the falling-factorial basis $r(r-1),\ r,\ 1$; then $\frac{r(r-1)}{r!}=\frac1{(r-2)!}$ and $\frac{r}{r!}=\frac1{(r-1)!}$.
Operator view: $\left(x\frac{d}{dx}\right)$ multiplies the coefficient of $x^r$ by $r$; $x^2\frac{d^2}{dx^2}$ multiplies by $r(r-1)$.
Sanity check: the $n=1$ term is $\frac{17}{3!}\approx2.83$ and later terms fall quickly, so a total near $3.06$ is reasonable.

concepts: Probability: classical definition with counting of arithmetic progressions
questions.question: Out of 11 consecutive natural numbers if three numbers are selected at random (without repetition), then the probability that they are in A.P. with positive common difference, is :
questions.key_idea: Count A.P.s by common difference $d$: the first term can be any of the first $11-2d$ numbers.
solution: Common difference $1$: the triple runs from $\{a_1,a_2,a_3\}$ to $\{a_9,a_{10},a_{11}\}$, so $9$ triples.

alternate_solutions.idea: Three numbers are in A.P. exactly when the outer two have the same parity (the middle one is their average).
solution: If $a<b<c$ are in A.P. then $b=\frac{a+c}{2}$, so $a+c$ is even: $a$ and $c$ have the same parity.
Conversely any two numbers $a<c$ of the same parity have an integer midpoint $b$ strictly between them.
So favourable triples correspond one-to-one with pairs of same parity. Among $1,\dots,11$: 6 odd and 5 even numbers.

useful_results: Number of 3-term A.P.s in $\{1,\dots,n\}$: $\left\lfloor\frac{(n-1)^2}{4}\right\rfloor$. Check $n=11$: $\frac{100}{4}=25$.
Three numbers $a<b<c$ are in A.P. $\iff a\equiv c\pmod2$ (then $b$ is forced); this reduces the count to pairs of equal parity: ${}^{\lceil n/2\rceil}C_2+{}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}C_2$.
Selection 'at random without repetition' of a set is unordered; a set in A.P. with $d>0$ has exactly one ordering, so no factor 6 or 2 appears.

concepts: Binomial coefficients: greatest value of $^nC_r$ and ratio of coefficients
questions.question: If $a$, $b$ and $c$ are the greatest values of ${}^{19}C_p$, ${}^{20}C_q$ and ${}^{21}C_r$ respectively, then :
questions.key_idea: $^nC_r$ is greatest at the middle $r$; relate neighbours with ${}^nC_r=\frac nr\,{}^{n-1}C_{r-1}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Pascal's rule plus symmetry: $^{20}C_{10}={}^{19}C_9+{}^{19}C_{10}=2\,{}^{19}C_9$, and similarly for $c$.

useful_results: ${}^nC_r$ is maximal at $r=\frac n2$ for even $n$, and at $r=\frac{n\pm1}{2}$ (two equal values) for odd $n$.
${}^nC_r=\frac nr\,{}^{n-1}C_{r-1}$ and $\frac{{}^nC_{r-1}}{{}^nC_r}=\frac{r}{n-r+1}$ turn any ratio of binomial coefficients into a product of simple fractions.

concepts: Total probability (two-stage experiment)
questions.question: An unbiased coin is tossed. If the outcome is a head then a pair of unbiased dice is rolled and the sum of the numbers obtained on them is noted. If the toss of the coin results in tail then a card from a well-shuffled pack of nine cards numbered $1,2,3,\dots,9$ is randomly picked and the number on the card is noted. The probability that the noted number is either 7 or 8 is:
questions.key_idea: Condition on the coin: weight each branch's probability of '7 or 8' by $\frac12$.
solution: Head (probability $\frac12$): the sum of two dice is 7 in 6 ways and 8 in 5 ways, so $P(\text{7 or 8}\mid H)=\frac{11}{36}$.
Tail (probability $\frac12$): one of the nine cards is picked, and 7 or 8 are 2 cards, so $P(\text{7 or 8}\mid T)=\frac29$.
useful_results: Law of total probability: $P(A)=\sum_iP(B_i)P(A\mid B_i)$ over a partition $\{B_i\}$ (here the coin: $H,T$).
Number of ways of getting a sum $s$ with two dice: $6-|s-7|$ for $2\le s\le12$ (sum 7: 6, sum 8: 5).
Draw a two-branch tree first; multiply along a path, add across the paths that satisfy the event.

concepts: Matrix powers (periodicity of a matrix)
Cube roots of unity
questions.question: Let $\alpha$ be a root of the equation $x^2+x+1=0$ and the matrix $A=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\1&\alpha&\alpha^2\\1&\alpha^2&\alpha^4\end{pmatrix}$, then the matrix $A^{31}$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Show $A^2$ is a permutation matrix, so $A^4=I$ and $A^{31}=A^{28}A^3=A^3$.
solution: Since $\alpha$ is a root of $x^2+x+1=0$, $\alpha$ is a primitive cube root of unity: $\alpha^3=1$, $1+\alpha+\alpha^2=0$, and $\alpha^4=\alpha$.
Each entry is a sum of three cube roots of unity: it is $3$ when the exponents add to a multiple of 3, else $0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $A$ is the normalised $3\times3$ discrete Fourier matrix; its square sends index $j$ to $-j\pmod 3$, a transposition, so $A^4=I$.
solution: Number rows and columns $0,1,2$: the $(j,k)$ entry of $\sqrt3A$ is $\alpha^{jk}$ (since $\alpha^4=\alpha^{2\cdot2}$).
This geometric sum is $3$ if $j+l\equiv0\pmod3$ and $\frac{1-\alpha^{3(j+l)}}{1-\alpha^{j+l}}=0$ otherwise.
So $A^2$ has a 1 exactly where $l\equiv-j$: it swaps indices $1\leftrightarrow2$ and fixes $0$, a permutation $P$ with $P^2=I$.
Hence $A^4=P^2=I$, so $A^{31}=A^{31-28}=A^3$. Option (B), the same answer.

useful_results: The normalised DFT matrix $F=\frac1{\sqrt n}\left(\omega^{jk}\right)$, $\omega=e^{2\pi i/n}$, is unitary, $F^2$ is the 'reversal' permutation $j\mapsto-j\pmod n$, and $F^4=I$ for every $n$.
For a primitive $n$-th root of unity $\omega$: $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\omega^{mk}=n$ if $n\mid m$, else $0$.
If $A^k=I$ then $A^m=A^{m\bmod k}$; always look for the smallest $k$ (here $A^2\neq I$, so $k=4$).
Check: $\mathrm{tr}A^2=1$ matches the trace of the permutation matrix (one fixed index).

concepts: Square root of a complex number
Real and imaginary parts
questions.question: The imaginary part of $\left(3+2\sqrt{-54}\right)^{\frac12}-\left(3-2\sqrt{-54}\right)^{\frac12}$ can be :
questions.key_idea: $3\pm6\sqrt6\,i=\left(3\pm\sqrt6\,i\right)^2$, so both square roots are $\pm\left(3\pm\sqrt6\,i\right)$.
solution: The difference is $\pm(3+\sqrt6\,i)\mp(3-\sqrt6\,i)$ with independent signs: $\pm2\sqrt6\,i$ or $\pm6$.
The imaginary part is therefore $\pm2\sqrt6$ (or $0$ in the real cases $\pm6$), so $-2\sqrt6$ is possible. Option (D).
questions.correction_note: PDF's first line prints $\left(3+2\sqrt{54}\right)^{1/2}$ on the right-hand side of the final equation (missing the $-$ sign inside the root; should be $\sqrt{-54}$). It also states the imaginary part is $\pm2\sqrt6$ without noting that the two real values $\pm6$ have imaginary part $0$. Answer unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: The two radicands are conjugates, so the roots are $w$ and $\pm\bar w$; the difference is $2i\,\mathrm{Im}\,w$ or $2\,\mathrm{Re}\,w$.
solution: Let $z=3+6\sqrt6\,i$; the other radicand is $\bar z$. If $w^2=z$ then $\left(\bar w\right)^2=\bar z$, so the roots of $\bar z$ are $\pm\bar w$.
The expression is $\pm w\mp'\bar w$: either $w-\bar w=2i\,\mathrm{Im}(w)$ (purely imaginary) or $w+\bar w=2\,\mathrm{Re}(w)$ (real), up to sign.
Imaginary part of the expression: $\pm2\sqrt6$ in the first case, $0$ in the second. Hence $-2\sqrt6$ is possible. Option (D), the same answer.

useful_results: If $w=p+iq$ and $w^2=a+ib$ then $p^2=\frac{|a+ib|+a}{2}$, $q^2=\frac{|a+ib|-a}{2}$, and $\mathrm{sign}(pq)=\mathrm{sign}(b)$.
$\sqrt{a+ib}$ is a perfect square when $|a+ib|$ is a perfect square: here $|z|=15$ gave $9$ and $6$.
Radicands $z$ and $\bar z$ give $w$ and $\pm\bar w$, so $\sqrt z\pm\sqrt{\bar z}$ is $2\,\mathrm{Re}\sqrt z$ or $2i\,\mathrm{Im}\sqrt z$.
Every non-zero complex number has two square roots, $\pm w$; 'can be' questions need all sign choices.

concepts: Statistics: mean and variance of combined data
questions.question: The mean and variance of a set of 15 numbers are 12 and 14 respectively. The mean and variance of another set of 15 numbers are 14 and $\sigma^2$ respectively. If the variance of all the 30 numbers in the two sets is 13, then $\sigma^2$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Combined variance $=\frac{n_1\sigma_1^2+n_2\sigma_2^2}{n_1+n_2}+\frac{n_1n_2(m_1-m_2)^2}{(n_1+n_2)^2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Take deviations from the combined mean: each set's mean is exactly 1 away from 13, so $13=\frac12\left[(14+1)+(\sigma^2+1)\right]$.
solution: Total variance $=$ average over the sets of $\left[\text{variance}+(\text{mean}-13)^2\right]$.

useful_results: Combined variance $=$ (weighted average of the variances) $+$ (weighted variance of the means); for equal sizes the second term is $\frac{(m_1-m_2)^2}{4}$.
Equivalently $\sigma^2=\frac{\sum n_i\left[\sigma_i^2+(m_i-M)^2\right]}{\sum n_i}$ where $M$ is the combined mean.
Raw-sum check: $\sum x^2=n(\sigma^2+m^2)$ for each set; here $15\cdot158+15(196+10)=5460=30\cdot(13^2+13)$.

concepts: Regions in the Argand plane (disc, half-planes)
questions.question:
Let $S_1$, $S_2$ and $S_3$ be three sets defined as
$S_1=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z-1|\le\sqrt2\}$, $S_2=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\mathrm{Re}\,((1-i)z)\ge1\}$, $S_3=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\mathrm{Im}(z)\le1\}$.
Then the set $S_1\cap S_2\cap S_3$ :
questions.key_idea: Translate each set into $x,y$: a closed disc and two half-planes; their overlap has non-empty interior.
solution: On the figure the disc, the line $x+y=1$ and the line $y=1$ cut out a shaded region with non-empty interior.
A region with interior contains infinitely many points, so $S_1\cap S_2\cap S_3$ has infinitely many elements. Option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Skip the picture: exhibit an explicit infinite family inside all three sets.
solution: Every $t\in[0,1]$ gives a different point of the intersection, so it is infinite. Option (A), the same answer.

useful_results: With $z=x+iy$: $\mathrm{Re}\left((a+ib)z\right)=ax-by$, so $\mathrm{Re}\left((1-i)z\right)=x+y$.
A system of inequalities with a strict interior point (or a segment) has infinitely many solutions; finitely many solutions arise only at tangent/touching positions.
Quick test of non-emptiness: check a convenient point such as the disc's centre or a point on a boundary line; here $\left(1,\tfrac12\right)$ is inside all three.

concepts: Locus in the Argand plane (difference of squared distances is a line)
Intercepts of a line
questions.question: Let $z_1=2+3i$ and $z_2=3+4i$. The set $S=\left\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z-z_1|^2-|z-z_2|^2=|z_1-z_2|^2\right\}$ represents a :
options: straight line with the sum of its intercepts on the coordinate axes equals $-18$
straight line with the sum of its intercepts on the coordinate axes equals 14
hyperbola with the length of the transverse axis 7
questions.answer: (C) straight line with the sum of its intercepts on the coordinate axes equals 14
questions.key_idea: The squares of $x$ and $y$ cancel, leaving a straight line.
solution: This is a straight line with intercepts $7$ and $7$ on the axes; their sum is $14$. Option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: The condition is Pythagoras: $|z-z_1|^2=|z-z_2|^2+|z_2-z_1|^2$ means a right angle at $z_2$, so $z$ lies on the perpendicular to $z_1z_2$ through $z_2$.
solution: By the converse of Pythagoras the triangle with vertices $z,z_2,z_1$ has a right angle at $z_2$, i.e. $(z-z_2)\perp(z_1-z_2)$.
So $z$ lies on the line through $z_2=(3,4)$ perpendicular to $z_1z_2$, whose direction is $(1,1)$; the line has normal $(1,1)$.
The line is $1(x-3)+1(y-4)=0$, i.e. $x+y=7$ (the degenerate point $z=z_2$ is on it).

useful_results: $|z-z_1|^2-|z-z_2|^2=k$ is always a straight line perpendicular to $z_1z_2$ (the $|z|^2$ terms cancel); $k=0$ gives the perpendicular bisector.
$|z-z_1|^2-|z-z_2|^2=|z_1-z_2|^2$ is the line through $z_2$ perpendicular to $z_1z_2$.
Intercepts of $ax+by=c$ on the axes are $\frac ca$ and $\frac cb$; for $x+y=7$ both equal 7.
Conics need $|z-z_1|\pm|z-z_2|=k$ (ellipse/hyperbola); squares of distances alone cannot give a hyperbola.

concepts: Modulus of a complex number and the circle $|z-z_1|=k|z-z_2|$
Greatest integer function
questions.question: Let $a,b$ be two real numbers such that $ab<0$. If the complex number $\frac{1+ai}{b+i}$ is of unit modulus and $a+ib$ lies on the circle $|z-1|=2|z|$, then a possible value of $\frac{1+[a]}{4b}$, where $[t]$ is the greatest integer function, is :
questions.answer: Dropped in the PDF - no option matches (computed values: $0$ or $-\frac{1+\sqrt7}{4}$)
questions.key_idea: Unit modulus gives $|a|=|b|$, so $b=-a$; the circle condition then fixes $a$ by a quadratic.
solution: Case $a=\frac{-1-\sqrt7}{6}\approx-0.608$: $b=\frac{1+\sqrt7}{6}$ and $[a]=-1$, so $1+[a]=0$ and the value is $0$.
The possible values are $-\frac{1+\sqrt7}{4}$ and $0$; none equals $\pm\frac12$ or $\pm1$, so no option matches (the PDF drops the question).
questions.correction_note: PDF stops after the first case ('Similarly it is not matching with $a=\frac{-1-\sqrt7}{6}$') without computing the second case. The second case is now written out: $[a]=-1$, so the value is $0$. Verified numerically; the key 'Drop' is right for the printed question. (If the stem were read as $1+\frac{[a]}{4b}$, the case $[a]=0$ would give $1$, option (C), which is probably what the author intended.)

alternate_solutions.idea: Skip solving the quadratic: the sign of $b$ and the value of $[a]$ show that no option can occur, and a direct substitution rejects the rest.
solution: As before $b=-a$ and $a$ satisfies $6a^2+2a-1=0$. The sum of the roots is $-\frac13$ and the product $-\frac16$, so one root is positive and one negative.
The circle $|z-1|=2|z|$ gives $3(x^2+y^2)+2x-1=0$: centre $\left(-\frac13,0\right)$, radius $\frac23$, so $-1\le a\le\frac13$ and $[a]\in\{-1,0\}$.
If $[a]=-1$ the numerator $1+[a]=0$, so the value is $0$, which is not an option.
If $[a]=0$ then $0\le a<1$, so $b=-a<0$ and the value $\frac{1}{4b}<0$: only $-\frac12$ or $-1$ could occur, i.e. $b=-\frac12$ or $b=-\frac14$.
So no option occurs: the question has no correct option (same conclusion).

useful_results: $\left|\frac{p+qi}{r+si}\right|=1\iff p^2+q^2=r^2+s^2$; here $1+a^2=b^2+1$.
Apollonius circle: $|z-z_1|=k|z-z_2|$ with $k\ne1$ is a circle; for $|z-1|=2|z|$ it has centre $-\frac13$ and radius $\frac23$ (so $x\in[-1,\frac13]$).
When an answer is requested 'a possible value', list all cases (here two roots, two values of $[a]$) before matching options.
Check readings of the stem: $\frac{1+[a]}{4b}$ and $1+\frac{[a]}{4b}$ differ; the second would give $1$ for $[a]=0$.

concepts: Locus in the Argand plane (Möbius transformation)
Distance between intercepts of a curve
questions.question: Let $u=\frac{2z+i}{z-ki}$, $z=x+iy$ and $k>0$. If the curve represented by $\mathrm{Re}(u)+\mathrm{Im}(u)=1$ intersects the $y$-axis at the points $P$ and $Q$ where $PQ=5$, then the value of $k$ is :
questions.key_idea: Put $x=0$ in the curve: it becomes a quadratic in $y$ whose root difference is $PQ$.
solution: Remark: $y^2+y-k-k^2=(y-k)(y+k+1)$; the root $y=k$ is the pole $z=ki$ of $u$, which the question takes as a point of the curve (its closure), so the chord is $|2k+1|=5$.
questions.correction_note: Working and answer are right for the intended question. Gap filled with a final remark: the quadratic $y^2+y-k-k^2=(y-k)(y+k+1)$ has the root $y=k$, i.e. $z=ki$, where $u$ is undefined (denominator zero), so strictly the curve itself meets the $y$-axis only at $y=-k-1$; the question intends the curve's closure through $z=ki$, and $PQ=|2k+1|=5$ gives $k=2$ as keyed. Checked with sympy.

alternate_solutions.idea: Divide first: $u=2+\frac{(2k+1)i}{z-ki}$, which turns the curve into a circle through $ki$ with a simple intercept chord.

useful_results: Divide the numerator by the denominator before substituting: $\frac{az+b}{z-c}=a+\frac{b+ac}{z-c}$; then the real and imaginary parts have the same denominator and are easy.
Real and imaginary parts of $\frac{1}{z-w}$ are $\frac{x-p}{\rho^2}$ and $\frac{-(y-q)}{\rho^2}$ with $w=p+iq$.
A condition $\mathrm{Re}\,u+\mathrm{Im}\,u=c$ for a Möbius $u$ is a circle (or line) through the pole.
Chord on $x=0$ of $y^2+By+C=0$: length $\sqrt{B^2-4C}$; here $B=1,C=-k-k^2$ gives $2k+1$.

concepts: Coordinate geometry: area of a triangle with a vertex at the origin
Counting divisors of an integer
questions.question: Let $S$ be the set of all triangles in the $xy$-plane, each having one vertex at the origin and the other two vertices lie on coordinate axes with integral coordinates. If each triangle in $S$ has area 50 sq. units, then the number of elements in the set $S$ is :
questions.key_idea: Area $\frac12|ab|=50$ forces $|ab|=100$; count divisors of 100 and signs.
solution: The vertices are $O(0,0)$, $A(a,0)$ and $B(0,b)$ on the axes with $a,b$ non-zero integers.
Number of positive divisors $=3\times3=9$, so $9$ choices of $|a|$ (and then $|b|=\frac{100}{|a|}$).
Each of $a$ and $b$ can be positive or negative: $4$ sign choices.
useful_results: Number of positive divisors of $p^{\alpha}q^{\beta}$ is $(\alpha+1)(\beta+1)$; for $100=2^25^2$ it is $9$.
Triangle $O(0,0),A(a,0),B(0,b)$ has area $\frac12|ab|$; distinct pairs $(a,b)$ (with signs) give distinct triangles.
Integer solutions of $|ab|=N$ with $ab\ne0$: $4\,\tau(N)$ (here $4\times9=36$); for $ab=N>0$ exactly it is $2\,\tau(N)$.

concepts: Remainder theorem with binomial expansion (divisibility)
questions.question: The remainder when $\left((64)^{(64)}\right)^{(64)}$ is divided by 7 is equal to :
questions.key_idea: $64=63+1=1+9\cdot7$, so every power of 64 leaves remainder 1.

solution: The remainder is $1$. Option (D), the same answer.

useful_results: If $a\equiv1\pmod m$ then $a^n\equiv1\pmod m$ for every $n\ge0$; $64\equiv1\pmod 7$ and $\pmod 9$ and $\pmod{21}$ as $63=7\cdot9$.
Reduce the base first; a huge exponent tower is irrelevant when the base is $\equiv1$ (or $\equiv-1$: sign $(-1)^n$).
General: $(1+km)^n=1+m(\dots)$, so $(1+km)^n\equiv1\pmod m$.

concepts: Binomial theorem: coefficient extraction
Sum of binomial coefficients (hockey-stick identity)
questions.question: The coefficient of $x^{70}$ in $x^2(1+x)^{98}+x^3(1+x)^{97}+x^4(1+x)^{96}+\dots+x^{54}(1+x)^{46}$ is ${}^{99}C_p-{}^{46}C_q$. Then a possible value of $p+q$ is :
questions.key_idea: Each term gives ${}^{n}C_{30}$ with $n=98,97,\dots,46$; sum them with the hockey-stick identity.
solution: Coefficient of $x^{70}$ in $x^k(1+x)^{100-k}$ is the coefficient of $x^{70-k}$ in $(1+x)^{100-k}$, i.e. ${}^{100-k}C_{70-k}$.
Using symmetry, $p\in\{31,68\}$ and $q\in\{31,15\}$, so $p+q\in\{62,99,46,83\}$; among the options only $83$ occurs ($p=68$, $q=15$). Option (B).
questions.correction_note: PDF writes the possible values as '62, 83, 99, 46' without saying how they arise, and its last lines (${}^{99}C_{31}-{}^{46}C_{31}={}^{99}C_p-{}^{46}C_q$) skip the use of symmetry; the step choosing $p\in\{31,68\},q\in\{15,31\}$ is added. All values verified by brute force: coefficient $={}^{99}C_{31}-{}^{46}C_{31}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The series is geometric with ratio $\frac{x}{1+x}$; sum it in closed form, then read the coefficient directly.
solution: So $p=68$, $q=15$ and $p+q=83$ (also valid: $p=31$, $q=31$ gives $62$, etc.). Option (B), the same answer.

useful_results: Series $\sum x^k(1+x)^{m-k}$ is geometric with ratio $\frac{x}{1+x}$: $\sum_{k=a}^{b}x^k(1+x)^{m-k}=x^a(1+x)^{m-a+1}-x^{b+1}(1+x)^{m-b}$.
${}^nC_r={}^nC_{n-r}$ means 'possible values' of subscripts come in pairs $r,\,n-r$.
Check: $a=b=2$, $m=4$ gives $x^2(1+x)^3-x^3(1+x)^2=x^2(1+x)^2$, as it should.

concepts: Binomial coefficients: ratios of consecutive coefficients
Locus of the centroid of a triangle (circle)
questions.question: Let ${}^nC_{r-1}=28$, ${}^nC_r=56$ and ${}^nC_{r+1}=70$. Let $A(4\cos t,4\sin t)$, $B(2\sin t,-2\cos t)$ and $C(3r-n,\,r^2-n-1)$ be the vertices of a triangle $ABC$, where $t$ is a parameter. If $(3x-1)^2+(3y)^2=\alpha$ is the locus of the centroid of triangle $ABC$, then $\alpha$ equals :
questions.key_idea: Consecutive-coefficient ratios give $n=8,r=3$; then $A\perp B$ so $|A+B|$ is constant and the centroid traces a circle.
solution: Centroid $(x,y)$: $x=\frac{4\cos t+2\sin t+1}{3}$ and $y=\frac{4\sin t-2\cos t+0}{3}$.
So $3x-1=4\cos t+2\sin t$ and $3y=4\sin t-2\cos t$.
Square and add: $(3x-1)^2+(3y)^2=(16+4)\left(\cos^2t+\sin^2t\right)+\left(16\cos t\sin t-16\cos t\sin t\right)=20$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's working stops at '(r = 3), (n = 8)'; the centroid part of the question is not solved in the PDF at all. Written here: $C=(1,0)$, centroid coordinates and $(3x-1)^2+(3y)^2=20$. Answer B agrees with the key; checked with sympy.

alternate_solutions.idea: Row 8 of Pascal's triangle is $1,8,28,56,70$; and $\vec{OB}$ is $\vec{OA}$ turned through $-90^\circ$ and halved, so $|A+B|$ is constant.
solution: Recognise $28,56,70$ as consecutive entries of row $n=8$: ${}^8C_2,{}^8C_3,{}^8C_4$, so $r-1=2$, $r=3$, $n=8$.
$\vec{OA}\cdot\vec{OB}=(4\cos t)(2\sin t)+(4\sin t)(-2\cos t)=0$, so $OA\perp OB$ with $|OA|=4$ and $|OB|=2$.
With $C=(1,0)$: $(3x-1)^2+(3y)^2=20$. So $\alpha=20$. Option (B), the same answer.

useful_results: For consecutive coefficients $\frac{{}^nC_{r}}{{}^nC_{r-1}}=\frac{n-r+1}{r}$; two ratios give two linear equations in $n,r$.
If $\vec a\perp\vec b$ then $|\vec a+\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2+|\vec b|^2$: $(4\cos t,4\sin t)$ and $(2\sin t,-2\cos t)$ are perpendicular vectors of lengths $4,2$.
Centroid locus when two vertices move on a circle-like path and the third is fixed is a circle: $3G-C=A+B$.
$(p\cos t+q\sin t)^2+(p\sin t-q\cos t)^2=p^2+q^2$ for all $t$.

concepts: Bayes' theorem (conditional probability)
questions.question: In a group of 400 people, 160 are smokers and non-vegetarian; 100 are smokers and vegetarian and the remaining 140 are non-smokers and vegetarian. Their chances of getting a particular chest disorder are 35%, 20% and 10% respectively. A person is chosen from the group at random and is found to be suffering from the chest disorder. The probability that the selected person is a smoker and non-vegetarian is :
questions.key_idea: Bayes' theorem: weight each group by its size and its chance of the disorder.
solution: The three groups are $E_1$: smokers and non-vegetarian ($160$), $E_2$: smokers and vegetarian ($100$), $E_3$: non-smokers and vegetarian ($140$); let $D$ be the disorder.
useful_results: Bayes: $P(E_i\mid D)=\frac{P(E_i)P(D\mid E_i)}{\sum_jP(E_j)P(D\mid E_j)}$; group sizes can replace probabilities because the common factor $\frac1{400}$ cancels.
Sanity check: the three posteriors $\frac{56}{90},\frac{20}{90},\frac{14}{90}$ add to 1.
Expected number of sufferers: $56+20+14=90$ of 400; the answer is the share of group 1 among them.

concepts: Geometric progression condition
Probability: sum of two dice
questions.question: Let $N$ be the sum of the numbers appeared when two fair dice are rolled and let the probability that $N-2,\ \sqrt{3N},\ N+2$ are in geometric progression be $\frac{k}{48}$. Then the value of $k$ is
questions.key_idea: Three terms are in G.P. iff the middle squared equals the product of the outer terms, giving $N=4$.
solution: $N=-1$ is rejected (a sum of two dice is at least 2).
useful_results: $a,b,c$ are in G.P. iff $b^2=ac$ (for non-zero terms); in A.P. iff $2b=a+c$.
Ways to get sum $s$ with two dice: $6-|s-7|$; sum $4$ gives $3$.
For $N=4$ the terms $2,\sqrt{12},6$ have ratio $\sqrt3$, confirming the G.P.

concepts: Binomial distribution: mean and standard deviation
questions.question: A bag contains 30 white balls and 10 red balls. 16 balls are drawn one by one randomly from the bag with replacement. If $X$ be the number of white balls drawn, then $\left(\frac{\text{mean of }X}{\text{standard deviation of }X}\right)$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Drawing with replacement makes $X$ binomial with $n=16$, $p=\frac34$.
useful_results: $B(n,p)$: mean $np$, variance $npq$; the ratio mean/s.d. is $\sqrt{\frac{np}{q}}$ ($=\sqrt{16\cdot3}=4\sqrt3$ here).
'With replacement' keeps $p$ constant, giving a binomial; 'without replacement' gives a hypergeometric distribution with smaller variance.
Mean $>$ variance for every binomial ($q<1$); this is a quick test for the distribution.

concepts: Conditional probability for nested events
questions.question: Let $A$ and $B$ be two non-null events such that $A\subset B$. Then, which of the following statements is always correct?
questions.key_idea: $A\subset B$ gives $A\cap B=A$, so $P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A)}{P(B)}\ge P(A)$ because $P(B)\le1$.
solution: So $P\left(\frac AB\right)\ge P(A)$. Option (C). (Options A, B, D hold only in special cases.)

alternate_solutions.idea: Elimination by a counterexample: a die with $A=\{1\}\subset B=\{1,2\}$.
solution: Take one die: $A=\{1\}$, $B=\{1,2\}$, so $A\subset B$ with $P(A)=\frac16$, $P(B)=\frac13$ and $P(A\mid B)=\frac12$.
(C): $\frac12\ge\frac16$ holds; and for $B$ equal to the whole space, $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$ so (C) holds with equality. Only (C) survives. Option (C), the same answer.

useful_results: If $A\subset B$: $P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A)}{P(B)}\ge P(A)$, with equality iff $P(B)=1$ (or $P(A)=0$); also $P(B\mid A)=1$.
Conditioning on an event that contains $A$ can only raise the probability of $A$ (the sample space shrinks).
Quick test of 'always true' statements: try one nested pair on a die, e.g. $A=\{1\}\subset B=\{1,2\}$.
